html:
Follow-up queues and continuation attempts

A queued continuation is an instruction for the next successful boundary of one task lineage. Acceptance stores the instruction and its selected resources. The controller reads the preceding attempt's retained context when it dispatches the instruction, so work completed after enqueue remains available to the child. The selected carry-forward policy determines how that context reaches a model request; enqueue does not freeze a copy of the transcript.

The conversation coordinator advances queues even when every browser is closed. Browser queue reads and updates display state. They do not create a child or run the model. For controls and keyboard behavior, see the Chat tour; for retained context and explicit source reads, see Context.

For disclosure lifetime, revision-checked reads and deletion conflicts in the shared browser panel, see browser queue flows.

Owners

Owner Responsibility
Native queue Stores ordered intent, retry identity and queue revisions; atomically links a scheduled item to its continuation child.
Queue API Resolves scoped task requests, accepts resources, returns public snapshots and advances eligible roots under the coordinator lock.
Continuation service Validates task lane and saved execution identities, creates or recovers the native child, repairs presentation records and wakes execution.
Continuation transaction Owns the single-child gate, inherited task state, notebook/artifact scope, follow-up amendment and request/run lineage.
Instruction resources Captures resource intent and private accepted snapshots, then revalidates and applies them at the instruction's processing boundary.
Conversation coordinator Advances continuations before independent chat admission and reserves affected conversations during that pass.
Queue panel Displays counts/items, manages disclosure and deletion feedback, coalesces reads and ignores obsolete responses after disposal.

Acceptance and order

POST /api/agent/native/{request_id}/follow-up-queue accepts amendment, submission_id and optional resources. Public resources contain context and Gateway IDs; accepted parameter records come from explicit references in the instruction text. The route checks accepted terms, prompt syntax and task retirement, then holds the task-queue lock while capturing resources and enqueueing.

Native acceptance enforces these limits:

  • The instruction must contain non-whitespace text, at most 24,000 characters. A leading slash after whitespace is an application command and cannot be queued.
  • A submission ID has 1–128 characters. Its digest binds the exact text and selected context/Gateway IDs. Resource-list ordering is retained after deduplication.
  • Each lineage permits 32 queued items. Scheduled items no longer contribute to that limit or the public queued count.
  • A submission ID cannot be rebound to a different root or digest, or collide with an accepted steer/follow-up submission. Exact retries return the original row, including a cancelled or started status, without requeueing it.

All attempts in the lineage share root_run_id. Sequence numbers increase within that root; cancelling a middle item leaves the relative order of the others unchanged. Roots are considered in sorted identity order, not by a global enqueue timestamp. The queue does not promise global FIFO ordering across independent tasks.

Resource acceptance recovers an existing submission snapshot before consulting live stores. For a new instruction, it checks current context grants, the combined 16-source attachment limit, selected Gateway scope and the merged parameter budget. It captures model routing at enqueue. A later parameter edit therefore cannot silently replace the value accepted for this instruction.

Parameter acceptance captures a snapshot without recording usage at this boundary. The merged-context check rejects unresolved references before applying an instruction; an unknown @parameter must not be assumed to become ordinary literal text. Resource acceptance and eventual parameter-use accounting are separate operations.

Acceptance sequence

sequenceDiagram participant U as Queue client participant A as Scoped queue API participant R as Instruction resource owner participant Q as Native queue transaction participant C as Conversation coordinator U->>A: Instruction, submission ID and selected resource IDs A->>A: Check terms, syntax, task retirement and queue lock A->>R: Recover exact accepted snapshot or validate new resources R-->>A: Recovered resource record or newly accepted snapshot A->>A: Capture model-routing snapshot A->>Q: Enqueue text, root, resources and routing alt Matching submission already exists Q-->>A: Return its retained status without requeueing else New valid intent Q->>Q: Check tombstone, identity collisions and pending limit Q->>Q: Publish root sequence, item and queue revision together Q-->>A: Queued receipt end A->>C: Publish invalidation and wake coordinator A-->>U: Public item status and queue snapshot Note over A,Q: Observer or response failure does not undo accepted intent

Retry identity is checked against retained records before live resources are consulted. Cancelled or started rows may have cleared their private resource payloads, but keep their identity and status. New settings cannot requeue those items. Conflicting reuse fails before a second item is admitted. The public snapshot projects labels and keys from the accepted record, rather than exposing its private parameter values. Nothing in this acceptance path copies the future parent checkpoint or dispatches the queued instruction.

Dispatch and recovery

flowchart TD A[Accept text resources and routing] --> Q[Queued item under lineage root] Q --> H{Head successful and ownership released?} H -->|No| W[Retain queued instruction] W --> H H -->|Yes| C{Capacity and task admission available?} C -->|No| W C -->|Yes| N[One native transaction: child plus scheduled item] N --> P[Repair task trace chat and event records] P --> S[Mark item started and wake native worker] N -->|Interrupted before repair finishes| R[Retry scheduled item using committed child] R --> P S --> B[Apply accepted resources before child's next decision] B --> M[Native worker continues task]

Scheduling and projection repair

sequenceDiagram participant C as Coordinator under capacity lock participant Q as Root queue and native transaction participant S as Continuation admission service participant P as Task and presentation stores participant W as Native continuation worker C->>Q: Read earliest queued or scheduled item per root alt Newly queued item C->>C: Require successful unowned head C->>C: Reserve this conversation before independent task admission C->>C: Require available capacity for a new child C->>S: Start attempt from the current head and saved item S->>S: Check lane, settling work and saved target/model identity S->>Q: Schedule with current carry policy and accepted routing Q->>Q: Read latest parent and validate FIFO plus root identity Q->>Q: Commit one child, amendment, evidence links and scheduled item Q-->>S: Child run and request identity else Scheduled item from an interrupted earlier pass C->>S: Recover using the item's original parent request S->>Q: Reuse committed child through the same identity gate Q-->>S: Same child identity end S->>P: Repair attempt, trace, conversation, event and current-run projections S->>Q: Mark scheduled item started and clear queue text/resources S->>P: Publish run/task invalidations S->>W: Wake existing native worker Note over Q,W: Started acknowledges repair, not model or workload execution

Automatic dispatch requires the latest attempt to be completed or answered and no longer owned. Failed, cancelled, interrupted, partial and blocked attempts hold the queue; waiting/paused or still-active attempts also do not dispatch. An explicit follow-up can recover an unsuccessful terminal attempt. After that recovery succeeds, the queued instruction uses the recovered context. A direct follow-up on a successful head with queued items is rejected with a request to use Queue, preserving pending order.

Before first creation, the continuation service checks task/head identity, the conversation lane, settling worker/trace state, cancellation and saved target/model availability. Saved Gateway identity selects the target; changing a default does not retarget the parent. The carry-forward policy is resolved at dispatch, whereas queued model routing comes from the accepted item. Direct native callers can instead supply their own resolved carry policy or inherit the parent's policy.

The native queue transaction reads the successful parent, verifies its root and the earliest queued sequence, and calls create_continuation using the same transaction. That owner permits exactly one child per parent. It commits the new run, request alias, lineage, follow-up amendment and retained evidence links before the queue item becomes visible as scheduled.

Task-attempt reservation, trace restoration, conversation turns, event occurrence updates and current-run projections follow the native commit. They are separate repairable operations. If a response or projection write is interrupted, the next pass reuses the scheduled item's parent and committed child. Recovery of an already scheduled item is not gated by a fresh available-slot check in the queue scanner; the shared continuation service still applies its task/lane rules.

started means the service reached its projection-repair acknowledgement. It does not certify model dispatch or successful workload execution. Actual execution is owned by the native continuation worker, whose wakeup follows admission.

HTTP admission failures save a visible hold reason when it changes. Expected 404/409/503 holds do not generate exception logs; other HTTP failures and unexpected exceptions are logged. Unexpected failures leave intent for another coordinator pass. Removed or archived tasks retire outstanding intent. Tombstoned roots are skipped by the scanner and remain subject to the deletion owners.

What the child inherits

The continuation owner copies explicit task/context allowlists rather than every parent field. These include accepted policies, task evidence, notebook identity, resource scope and retained context. It resets attempt counters, usage, pending control state and wall deadline, and strips temporary credential handles. A routing snapshot supplied for a new follow-up clears the inherited effective-model and inference-profile caches so the accepted routing can take effect.

The transaction rejects an owned parent, unresolved pending invocation, invalid provider message pairing, unavailable retained artifact, stale approval grant or obsolete shared-conversation head. Continue and Restart share the single-child identity gate; a retry cannot branch a parent that already has a child. Restart uses the dedicated fresh-attempt owner before inheriting the supported durable scope. Capability/resource grants additionally resolve the parent's approved wait inside the same native transaction.

Historical jobs remain observations of their original executions. Ownership and receipt claims do not transfer to the child. Nonterminal inherited jobs create unknown-operation records, and resource/dependency conflict checks can block new mutations until those effects are reconciled. Creating a child does not replay them.

flowchart TD Parent[Settled parent checkpoint at dispatch] --> Gate[Single-child identity and ownership gate] Queue[Accepted instruction, resources and routing] --> Gate Carry[Carry policy resolved at dispatch] --> Gate Gate --> Existing{Exact committed child already exists?} Existing -->|Yes| Repair[Return same identity for projection repair] Existing -->|No| Copy[Copy explicit task and context allowlists] Copy --> Scope[Preserve selected hosts, policies and permitted resource scope] Copy --> Evidence[Link retained artifacts and notebook lineage] Copy --> History[Keep historical jobs and unresolved-effect observations] Copy --> Fresh[Reset attempt counters, usage, pending controls and wall deadline] Fresh --> Strip[Remove temporary credential handles] Queue --> Amendment[Store child amendment and exact submission receipt] Scope --> Commit[Commit child, request alias and parent-child link together] Evidence --> Commit History --> Commit Strip --> Commit Amendment --> Commit Commit --> Worker[Owned native recovery and input processing] History --> Guard[Unresolved effects still constrain conflicting mutations] Guard --> Worker

This diagram shows ordinary continuation inheritance. Restart delegates to fresh_attempt before applying supported lineage rules. A follow-up with Automatic capability selection clears the prior selection result and initially exposes only required tools within the captured ceiling; the new input must obtain its own selection. This does not widen the parent's accepted authority. The selection sequence explains that later step.

Resource application

The follow-up amendment carries its accepted snapshot to the child's normal instruction-processing boundary. Application verifies conversation scope, current attachment metadata/digests, selected Gateway identity and aggregate parameter budget again. A metadata digest comparison is not a fresh hash of every blob; see the storage boundary in Context.

Explicit parameter bindings replace matching normalized keys; unmentioned bindings remain. Additional Gateways expand the available selection while preserving the primary target and existing target scope fields. The code prepares updated authority, tool declarations, parameter context and secret inventory before publishing the live state/context changes. It preserves already discovered tools and does not rewrite contexts belonging to in-flight invocations.

The caller owns checkpointing and retry when an accepted resource becomes unavailable. For human-answer checkpoints, a resource ValueError pauses and saves the run before consuming the answer. Cancelling queued intent applies none of its resource changes. Browser snapshots expose context names/IDs, Gateway labels/IDs and parameter keys, not accepted parameter values.

sequenceDiagram participant L as Owned run lifecycle participant A as Retained amendment store participant R as Resource application participant V as Context and Gateway stores participant S as Run checkpoint L->>A: Claim next amendment after applied sequence A-->>L: Text and its accepted resource snapshot L->>R: Apply snapshot before consuming instruction text R->>V: Recheck conversation, attachment metadata and Gateway identities R->>R: Merge accepted parameter bindings and check aggregate limits alt Resource validation fails R-->>L: ValueError without publishing the new live projection L->>S: Save paused state and diagnostic Note over L,A: Applied sequence stays unchanged for recovery else Resource validation succeeds R->>R: Build authority, tool catalog and secret inventory R-->>L: Publish complete state/context delta L->>L: Append instruction and advance applied sequence L->>L: Open notebook epoch and update output/recovery intent L->>S: Save message, input sequence and observations L->>L: Continue Task Contract and selection checks end

run_lifecycle.py owns this processing boundary. Owned resume first reconciles effects, Activities and waits; prepare_turn also checks cancellation, pauses, blockers and budgets before applying ordinary pending amendments. A resource failure cannot be bypassed by merely constructing a child. Successful input processing still precedes model-capacity and decision acceptance.

Cancellation and browser state

GET returns the queue snapshot; DELETE .../follow-up-queue/{item_id} cancels only a still-queued item in the addressed root. A missing or wrong-root item returns 404. If scheduling won the transaction race, deletion returns 409 and the browser refreshes authoritative state. Repeated cancellation succeeds without resurrection.

Cancellation clears stored instruction text and its private resource snapshot, while retaining identity/digest and routing metadata. Starting an item similarly clears its text/resources from the queue row; the accepted child/amendment has its own retained state. Retiring queue intent does not itself cancel a previously committed child. Conversation deletion is a separate lifecycle operation.

A public snapshot's count includes queued rows only, while its item list can also include scheduled rows awaiting acknowledgement. Those scheduled rows are visible and undeletable. A count of zero alone does not prove that no child is starting. The panel accepts equal/newer revisions within a root, coalesces overlapping reads and refreshes open item lists on relevant native status/revision changes. Expansion is remembered by root only for this page lifetime. A superseded attempt hides its queue controls; disposal fences late responses without aborting the underlying fetch. Submission retry identity belongs to the composer, not the display panel. The instruction editor flows trace exact text/resource retry identity, immediate follow-up receipts and the separate steering application tracker.

flowchart TD Queued[Queued intent] --> Race{Which transaction commits first?} Race -->|Cancel| Cancelled[Cancelled with identity and digest retained] Race -->|Schedule| Scheduled[Scheduled with committed child identity] Scheduled --> Repair[Repair downstream admission projections] Repair --> Started[Started acknowledgement] Scheduled --> Delete[User deletion returns conflict] Delete --> Refresh[Refresh current queue snapshot] Cancelled --> Retry[Exact enqueue retry returns cancelled] Scheduled --> Recover[Scheduled recovery reuses the same child] Recover --> Repair Started --> Execution[Native worker owns execution and completion] Removed[Task removed or archived] --> Retire[Retire remaining queue intent] Retire --> Preserve[Already committed child keeps its own lifecycle]

The native transaction decides the cancel/schedule race. Cancelling a queued row does not rewind its sequence or release its submission identity for reuse. Retirement can also clear a scheduled row's private queue payload, but cannot erase the child's committed instruction or establish that it stopped executing.

Verification boundaries

Native queue tests cover order, context-at-dispatch, cancellation races, restart and server advancement without browser polling. The RAM wrapper runs shared transaction cases with runtime SQLite denied. Direct follow-up tests cover single-child identity, terminal statuses, lane ownership and presentation repair. Resource tests cover accepted snapshots, boundary application, scope and retention.

Continuity fixtures check exact preceding replies and accepted use of retained reasoning across carry modes; their apparent cleanup commands execute only in a fake Gateway. The browser cases mock queue responses to test layout, disclosure, conflict recovery and retry identity. Browser fixtures do not establish production scheduler or durability behavior. Current validation results and outstanding failures are recorded in the repository's documentation review status.
